title: Men as trees, walking (Mark 8:22–26)
hookLine: the only healing done in two stages
tomorrow: who do you say I am

cards: A broken arm, a broken heart, a bad year: some things get better slowly. There's a day when it's not fixed, but not what it was either. Blurry.
In between. Up to now in Mark, a word or a touch has been enough. Today it takes two.
The boat lands at Bethsaida, a town on the lake, and people bring Jesus a blind man and beg him to touch him.

teach.h: LED BY THE HAND OUT OF TOWN.
teach.b: First, the walk. Jesus takes the blind man by the hand and leads him out of the village: a guide walking slowly, watching the ground for both of them. He heals him away from the crowd, like the deaf man two days ago.
Second, the first try. He spits on the man's eyes, lays his hands on him, and asks if he sees anything. The man looks up.
In the Douay-Rheims: "I see men as it were trees, walking." Shapes. Tall blurs moving.
Better than dark, and not right yet.
Third, the second touch. Jesus lays his hands on his eyes again, and now the man sees all things clearly. Why two stages?
The Gospel doesn't say, so readers look at where Mark put the story. Just before it, the disciples in the boat: eyes that don't see.
Just after it, tomorrow's scene, where Peter gets the answer right and the meaning wrong.
Some readers hear this healing as a picture of the disciples themselves: they see something, men as trees, and they'll need a second touch. Fourth, the quiet mercy of it.

teach.h: I SEE MEN AS IT WERE TREES, WALKING.
teach.b: The man is honest. He doesn't pretend to see clearly to be polite; he says: blurry. And Jesus doesn't scold him.
He just touches him again. The Catechism speaks of conversion in a similar way, as an ongoing task, not a single moment: the second touch, and the third.

how: The Catechism speaks of conversion as an ongoing task rather than a single moment, and Catholics return to confession and prayer again and again; the anointing of the sick can be received more than once.

o: a blessing repeated to make it stronger
a second miracle for a different blind man
healing that came in two stages, not at once

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: the fishing town where it happens
disciples with eyes that don't see

s: Mark says Jesus lacked the power to heal all at once
the Gospel gives no reason for two stages. readers look at where Mark placed it.
Jesus spits on the man's eyes before the first touch
Mark says he spat on his eyes and laid his hands on him, then asked if he saw anything.
the man pretends he can see after the first touch
he says honestly that people look like trees walking.

games.q: you're the blind man. after the first touch you see blurry shapes moving like trees. Jesus asks if you see anything. what do you say?
o: yes, I see fine, thank you.
I see men like trees, walking.
games.why: "I see men as it were trees, walking." he tells the truth, and Jesus touches him again.

practice: Think of one thing in you that's healing slowly, a grief, a habit, a body, a friendship, and without grading it, say honestly where it is, the way the man did: it's blurry, it's better than before, it isn't done.
Rest your hands over your eyes for a few breaths. If you pray, ask for the second touch; if you don't, let it be halfway for now, without hurrying it.

wordCard.voice: Second touch. The touch that made the blurry shapes a blind man saw at Bethsaida go clear: healing that came in two stages. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: trees walking, what the man saw after the first touch.

carryVoice: Your line: healing in stages. Blurry is a stage, not a failure. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: I see men as it were trees, walking.
